\section{Some mathematical preliminaries}\label{sec:math-prelim}

The goal of this section is to collect the main definitions of the mathematical objects in this paper: the quantum $K$-theory with level structure (after Ruan and Zhang \cite{rz}), and the quasimap quantum $K$-theory \cite{kimcfm}. 

Before diving into the technicalities, we give a rough outline of the main ideas. 
The reader so inclined may skip this section at a first reading, and instead 
start with the examples for projective spaces, Grassmannians, and partial flag manifolds, 
presented in the following sections.

The two quantum theories mentioned above 
are defined using the usual blueprint in Gromov-Witten theory. 
For a compact space $X$, one considers a (compact) moduli space of maps to $X$, 
which is equipped with a virtual fundamental class, and with evaluation maps. 
One defines Gromov-Witten invariants by pulling back via the evaluation maps. 
In general there are many choices of moduli spaces which compactify maps 
$\mathbb{P}^1 \to X$. In cohomology, various choices usually lead to the 
same theory, because of the basic fact that a fundamental class of an 
algebraic variety only depends on a Zariski open dense set. However, 
this fails in $K$-theory, where fundamental classes are sensitive to the 
singularities on the boundary, and on the compactification itself. 
Therefore, different choices of moduli spaces may in principle lead to 
different theories. This was proved to actually happen in some cases - see, e.g., \cite{GY}.
In our paper we use the two most popular compatifications in Gromov-Witten theory, via
the moduli space of stable maps, and via quasimaps. In these cases, and (at least) 
for flag manifolds,
one expects that the two theories are in fact the same, possibly up to 
some changes of variables.

A further wrinkle in this paper is that we consider {\em twisted} versions of quantum K 
theories. 
In the study of twisted theories, pioneered by Coates and Givental \cite{cg}, 
the virtual fundamental class is further multiplied by a class obtained from a push-pull 
formula involving the evaluation maps and a map from the universal family to the moduli space in question. The twisted theories we consider, especially the Ruan-Zhang 
theory with level structure \cite{rz}, fit with the physics realization of the quantum $K$-theory in physics. 
As mentioned in the introduction, 
and as one can see in the sections with the examples, for flag manifolds 
there are easy relations between the Ruan-Zhang levels in math, and the Chern-Simons levels
in physics.

A more satisfactory mathematical explanation of the precise relationship between the 
levels in math and physics requires diving into the generating functions of the 
Gromov-Witten theories under consideration, namely the $J$ function for the 
stable map theory, and the $I$ function for the quasimap theory. We recall these definitions in below in this section, but postpone the more 
technical parts, along with the main mathematical results and their proofs, 
unil the last section of the paper.

\subsection{Stable map invariants}

Recall that for $X$ a projective manifold, $K(X)$ denotes the Grothendieck 
ring of vector bundles on $X$.  Let $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n,d}(X)$ 
be Kontsevich's moduli space of stable maps from curves of genus $g$ with $n$ 
marked points. It is equipped with evaluation maps 
$\mathrm{ev}_i: \overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n,d}(X) \to X$. The Kontsevich 
space may not be smooth, or of the expected dimension.  One constructs 
a virtual structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}^{vir}$. We refer to Lee's paper 
\cite{yp} for details. In the examples of interest in this paper, $g=0$, and $X$ is a flag manifold. In this case, the moduli space
$\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n,d}(X)$ is irreducible,
rational, with finite quotient singularities, and  
$\mathcal{O}^{vir}$ is the usual structure sheaf 
$\mathcal{O}_{\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n,d}(X)}$;
see \cite{fulton.pandharipande,kim.pandharipande}.





Given inputs $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n\in K(X)[\tau, \tau^{-1}]$, 
for $\tau$ an indeterminate,
the $K$-theoretic Gromov-Witten invariants (with descendants) of $X$
are defined by 
\begin{equation} \label{E:KGW-stable-map}
\langle \alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\rangle_{g,n,d}=\chi\left(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n,d}(X);\mathcal{O}^{vir}\otimes\prod_{i=1}^n ev_i^*\alpha_i(L_i)\right)
\end{equation}
Here $L_i$ denotes the line bundle whose fiber over a moduli point is the cotangent line at the $i$th marked point of the curve, and the notation $ev_i^*\alpha_i(L_i)$ means pull back elements of  $K(X)[\tau, \tau^{-1}]$
%$K(X)$ 
by $ev_i$, and replace the variable $\tau$ with $L_i$.


We will 
further augment our $K$-theory classes with additional variables, taken from some ground $\lambda-$algebra which we denote $\mathcal{A}$. The same definitions apply in this setting, with inputs being taken from  $K(X)[\tau, \tau^{-1}] \otimes \mathcal{A}$ with values in $\mathcal{A}$. If we work torus-equivariantly, we include the $T$-equivariant parameters into $\mathcal{A}$. 




\subsection{Quasimap invariants}\label{sec:qmaps}

We recall next the basic definitions of quasimap moduli spaces, due to Ciocan-Fontanine, Kim, and Maulik \cite{kimcfm}. 
Let $V$ be an affine variety (always a vector space in the examples we consider), acted on by a reductive group $G$. Choosing a  character $\theta$ of $G$ determines a stability condition and a GIT quotient $V//G:= V//_{\theta} G$. 
We make the assumptions that the stable and semistable loci coincide, and that the stable locus is smooth and has no isotropy. Under these hypotheses,
an $n$-pointed genus $g$ quasimap is a tuple
$(f,C,P,u)$ where:
\begin{itemize}
\item $C$ is a prestable genus-$g$, $n$-pointed curve;
\item $f$ is a map $C\to V/G$ (here $V/G$ is the stack quotient of $V$ by $G$, rather than the GIT quotient $V//G$, which is our target space). We require that $f$ maps the generic point of $C$ to the stable locus inside $V$. The finitely many points of $C$ mapping to the unstable locus are called \emph{base points};
\item $P$ is a principal $G$-bundle over $C$;
\item $u$ is a section $C\to P\times_G V$.
\end{itemize}

As with stable maps, quasimaps have a well-defined notion of degree. The degree of a quasimap is the homomorphism $Pic_G(V)\to \mathbb{Z}$ given by sending a line bundle $L$ to ${\rm deg}_C(u^*(P\times_G L))$. 


A quasimap is called \emph{prestable} if the marked points and nodes of $C$ are not base points. Let $L_\theta$ denote the line bundle on $V$ determining the GIT stability condition, which is induced by the character $\theta$ of $G$. $L_\theta$ induces a line bundle $\mathcal{L}_\theta$ on $C$ by $\mathcal{L}_\theta:=u^*(P\times_G L_\theta)$. Fix $\epsilon >0$ a rational number. A prestable map is $\epsilon$-stable if it satisfies the following two conditions: 
\begin{itemize}
    \item The ${\mathbb Q}$-Cartier divisor corresponding to the ``bundle'' $\omega_C(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i)\otimes (\mathcal{L}_\theta)^\epsilon$ is ample.
    \item $\epsilon l(x)\leq 1$ for all $x\in C$. Here $l(x)$ denotes the contact order of $x$ with the unstable locus. 
\end{itemize}
The moduli stack parametrizing $\epsilon$-stable quadruples $(C,f,P,u)$ is denoted by $Q^\epsilon_{g,n,d}(V//G)$.
Under the conditions on $V$ and $G$ outlined earlier, $Q^\epsilon_{g,n,d}(V//G)$ is a proper Deligne-Mumford stack with a perfect obstruction theory. 
The quasimap spaces have $n$ evaluation maps at the $n$ marked points, denoted by $ev_i: Q^\epsilon_{g,n,d}(V//G)\to V//G$. The evaluation maps are well-defined since prestability implies that base points do not coincide with marked points.~{The space $Q^\epsilon_{g,n,d}(V//G)$} admits a universal family 
\[ \pi: C^\epsilon \to Q^\epsilon_{g,n,d}(V//G)\]
and a universal {principal $G$ bundle $B \to C^\epsilon$}. Unlike the case of stable maps, the universal family is not constructed by adding a marked point; this also means that there is no universal evaluation map, due to presence of base points. 


Tseng-You in \cite{kquasimap} defined $K$-theoretic quasimap GW invariants using this space in the following way. The perfect obstruction theory induces a virtual structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}^\epsilon$, and invariants are defined as follows. 
For $\alpha_i\in K(V//G)$,
\begin{equation}\label{E:KGW-qmap}\langle \alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\rangle_{g,n,d}^\epsilon := 
\chi\left(Q^\epsilon_{g,n,d}(V//G);\mathcal{O}^\epsilon\otimes \prod_i ev_i^*\alpha_i\right).\end{equation}

As in the case of stable maps, one can also define gravitational descendent invariants, by inserting powers of $L_i$ into the correlator, where $L_i$ is the line bundle corresponding to the cotangent line to $C$ at the $i$th marked point. The corresponding inputs are elements of $K(V//G)[\tau, \tau^{-1}]$. 




In the case where the moduli space of stable quasimaps is empty, one can still define analogues to Gromov-Witten invariants using the  quasimap graph spaces, whose properties we describe below. 
(In case both spaces are defined, the GW theories are the same.) Our reference for the theory of these spaces is \cite{kquasimap}.
Let $QG_{0,n,d}^\epsilon(V//G)$ denote the quasimap graph space. It is the moduli space parametrizing pairs $(C,\phi)$ where $C$ is a genus-0 curve equipped with a $n-$pointed quasimap to $V//G$, and $\phi$ is a degree-1 map from $C$ to $\mathbb{P}^1$, which contracts all components except for a distinguished component $C_0\cong \mathbb{P}^1$. Like the quasimap space, it admits a virtual structure sheaf, a universal family, with a universal curve $C$ and a universal $G$-principal bundle $B$. The stable map $\phi$ determines evaluation maps:
$$ev_i:QG_{0,n,d}^\epsilon(V//G)\to V//G$$
in the same manner as for the usual quasimap spaces.
There is a $\mathbb{C}^*$-action given by the standard action on $C_0$.

The stability condition is identical to the stability condition for $C$, except that \[\omega_C\left(\sum_i x_i+\sum_i y_i\right)\otimes (\mathcal{L}_\theta)^\epsilon \] 
must be ample, where $x_i$ are the marked points and $y_i$ are the nodes of $C \setminus C_0$. 

There is distinguished component of the $\mathbb{C}^*-$fixed locus 
denoted $F_{n,d}^\epsilon$, which corresponds to the locus of curves where $C/C_0$ 
is attached to $C_0$ at exactly the point $0$, and all 
marked points lie away from $C_0$. This component has 
a distinguished marked point, corresponding to $0\in C_0$. 
We let $N_{n,d}^\epsilon$ denote the normal bundle 
to  $F_{n,d}^\epsilon$. In the limit $\epsilon\to0^+$, we 
omit superscripts on the fixed point locus and the normal bundle.



It was proven in \cite{kimcfm} that
in the limit $\epsilon\to \infty$, the space $F^\epsilon_{n,d}$ is 
$\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n+1,d}(V//G)$, and the contribution of this 
portion of the fixed locus to integrals on $QG$ computes 
genus-$0$ Gromov-Witten invariants. 
In the limit $\epsilon\to 0^+$, the quasimap spaces $Q^{0^+}_{0,n+1,d}(V//G)$ are in general empty, however the graph spaces $QG^{0^+}_{g,n,d}(V//G)$ are not, and the fixed locus $F_{n,d}$ remains well-defined, so it is used as a ``substitute" when constructing generating functions, as we will see in section \ref{sec:IJ}.

\subsection{Twistings and level structures}

Defining the level structure and stating the abelian/non-abelian correspondence for the level $I$-functions requires discussing twisted invariants, initially introduced for quantum cohomology by Coates and Givental in \cite{cg}. These invariants are defined for stable map quantum $K$-theory by Tonita in \cite{Tonita}. Their quasimap counterparts were defined in general by Zhang in \cite{wallcrossing}. (These are {\em twistings of type I}, in the language of Givental.)



An insertion into a Gromov-Witten invariant can be regarded as imposing a constraint on the behavior of the stable map at the corresponding marked point. Similarly, twistings can be thought of as imposing universal constraints on image of the entire curve. 

Let $\mathfrak{C}$ be a $K$-theoretic characteristic class in the sense of \cite[definition 6.1]{z}, and additionally satisfying the following properties: 
\begin{itemize}
    \item Multiplicativity: 
    for a short exact sequence of vector bundles $A$, $B$, $E$ 
    \begin{equation}
        0 \: \longrightarrow \: A \: \longrightarrow \: E \: \longrightarrow \: B \: \longrightarrow \: 0,
    \end{equation}
    then $\mathfrak{C}(E) = \mathfrak{C}(A) \, \mathfrak{C}(B)$.
    \item Invertibily: for $E$ a vector bundle, $\mathfrak{C}(E)$ is an invertible element in $K(X)\otimes \mathcal{A}$. 
\end{itemize}

Such a class $\mathfrak{C}$ is well-defined on elements of $K(X)$ by letting $\mathfrak{C}(-A):=\frac{1}{\mathfrak{C}(A)}$ for $A$ a vector bundle, and extending by multiplicativity. 


Given an invertible multiplicative $K$-theoretic characteristic class $\mathfrak{C}$ and an element $E\in K(X)$, twisted $K$-theoretic Gromov-Witten invariants are defined by modifying the virtual structure sheaf of the appropriate moduli space with a class depending on $\mathfrak{C}$ and $E$. 

\begin{defn}\label{twistdef} The
$K$-theoretic Gromov-Witten invariants with twisting given by $(\mathfrak{C},E)$ are defined by replacing $\mathcal{O}^{vir}$ with $\mathcal{O}^{vir}\otimes T_{(\mathfrak{C},E)}$
in equations \eqref{E:KGW-stable-map} and \eqref{E:KGW-qmap}, where $T_{(\mathfrak{C},E)}$ is defined differently depending on the chosen moduli space:
\begin{itemize}
    \item For stable maps (i.e., in \eqref{E:KGW-stable-map}) 
    \begin{equation}\label{E:TCE-stable-map} T_{(\mathfrak{C},E)}:=\mathfrak{C}(ft_*ev_{n+1}^*E) \/. \end{equation}
    These were introduced by Tonita in \cite{Tonita}.
    \item For quasimaps (i.e., in \eqref{E:KGW-qmap}), $E$ is induced by a $G$-representation $R$, and 
    \begin{equation}\label{E:TCE-qmap}T_{(\mathfrak{C},E)}:=\mathfrak{C}(\pi_*(B\times_G R)) \in K(Q^\epsilon_{g,n,d}(V//G)) \/. \end{equation}
     This difference is due to the universal family not having a well-defined evaluation map to the target space. These were defined in general by Ruan-Zhang in \cite{wallcrossing}. 
\end{itemize}
    
Multiple twistings can be taken in succession, given characteristic classes $\mathfrak{C}_i$ and $K$-theory elements $E_i$. The corresponding modification to the virtual structure sheaf is:
\begin{equation}\label{multtwistclass}
T_{((\mathfrak{C}_1,E_1),\dots,(\mathfrak{C}_k,E_k))}:= \bigotimes_iT_{(\mathfrak{C_i},E_i)} .
\end{equation}
We refer to such a theory as being twisted by $((\mathfrak{C}_1,E_1),\dots,(\mathfrak{C}_k,E_k))$.  
\end{defn}
We consider the following main examples of characteristic classes: 
\begin{itemize}
    \item Euler classes: Choose $\mathfrak{C}$ to be the class $Eu_\lambda$, defined on a vector bundle $F$ by  
    \[Eu_\lambda(F)= 1- \lambda F^* + \lambda^2 \wedge^2 F^* - \ldots \/.\]  
    \item Determinants: Choose $\mathfrak{C}$ to be the $\ell$th power of the determinant $\det(F)^\ell$, where $\ell$ is any integer. 
    \item Products of the above classes.
\end{itemize}

Twisting using the determinant was introduced by Ruan-Zhang in \cite{rz}, and 
the resulting invariants are referred to as quantum $K$-theoretic invariants with (Ruan-Zhang) 
level structure. A definition of these invariants, for both stable maps and 
quasimaps, is given below. 

\begin{defn}\label{defn:twisted-qk} Let $E_1, \ldots , E_k$ be vector bundles on $X$ and $\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_k$ be integers. The  $K$-theoretic GW invariants with level structure determined by 
\[ (E_1,\ell_1),\dots,(E_k,\ell_k)\]
are the $K$-theoretic Gromov-Witten invariants with twisting given by 
$$((\det{}^{-\ell_1},E_1), \dots, ((\det{}^{-\ell_k},E_k))$$ 
in the sense of definition~$\ref{twistdef}$. 


The virtual structure sheaves $\mathcal{O}^{vir}$ from equations \eqref{E:KGW-stable-map} and \eqref{E:KGW-qmap} are defined by the following modifications, for the stable map and quasimap theory respectively:


 

\begin{itemize}

\item In the stable map theory, the virtual structure sheaf from \eqref{E:KGW-stable-map} is tensored with
\begin{equation}\label{E:TCE-level-stable-map} \det(ft_*ev_{n+1}^*E_1)^{-\ell_1} \otimes \ldots \otimes 
\det(ft_*ev_{n+1}^*E_k)^{-\ell_k} \/.\end{equation}
where (recall) $ft:\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n+1,d}(X) \to \overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n,d}(X)$
is the forgetful map.

\item In the quasimap theory, for a GIT quotient $V//G$, 
let $R_i$ be the $G$-representation giving $E_i$, and let 
$\pi_*(B \times_G R_i)$ be the corresponding (virtual) bundle on the quasimap space. 
Then $\mathcal{O}^{vir}$ from \eqref{E:KGW-qmap} is tensored with
\begin{equation}\label{E:TCE-level-qmap} \det(\pi_*(B\times_G R_1))^{-\ell_1} \otimes \ldots \otimes 
\det(\pi_*(B\times_G R_k))^{-\ell_k} \/.\end{equation}


\end{itemize}
    
\end{defn} 

\begin{remark}
    To keep notation consistent with both \cite{rz} and other literature regarding level structures, and references on general twisted invariants (e.g. \cite{Tonita}), we have two notations for level structures. 

    A level structure given by the bundles $(E_1,\ell_1),\dots,(E_k,\ell_k)$, is, in the notation of Definition \ref{twistdef}, a twisting described by $((\det^{-\ell_1},E_1),\dots,(\det^{-\ell_k},E_k))$.
\end{remark}


If $g=0$, and in the case of the stable map invariants, it is proved in \cite{HK1} that twisted invariants of the kind described in definition \ref{twistdef} define a ring structure. To define the product, one first defines the pairing:
    \[(\!(a,b)\!)^{tw}:=\sum_{d \ge 0}  \chi\Bigl(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,2,d}(X); \mathrm{ev}_1^*(a) \otimes \mathrm{ev}_2^*(b) \otimes T_{(\mathfrak{C},E)}\Bigr) q^d \/. \]
Then the product $\star$ is uniquely determined by the (Frobenius) condition:
\[ (\!(a\star b, c)\!)^{tw} = \sum_{d \ge 0}  \chi\Bigl(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,3,d}(X); \mathrm{ev}_1^*(a) \otimes \mathrm{ev}_2^*(b) \otimes \mathrm{ev}_3^*(c) \otimes T_{(\mathfrak{C},E)}\Bigr) q^d \/. \]



\subsection{(Small) $I$ and $J$ functions}  \label{sec:IJ}


Given a target space $X$, and a twisting determined by a class $\mathfrak{C}$ and 
a bundle $E$ we recall next the definition of the (twisted) small $I$ and 
$J$-functions of $X$, which are certain generating functions for the quasimap 
invariants (at $\epsilon=0$), and stable map invariants, respectively. 
Let $\phi^\alpha,\phi_\alpha$ denote twisted- Poincare dual bases for $K(X)$. We introduce the Novikov ring as the semigroup ring of the effective curve classes in $X$, generated by Novikov variables $q_i$, where $q_i$ are the elements corresponding to a chosen set of generators $g_i\in H_2(X)$. For any effective curve class $d=\sum_{i}d_ig_i$, we use $q^d$ as shorthand for $\prod_i q_i^{d_i}$.


The small (twisted) $K$-theoretic $J$-function of $X$ is (as per the definition in \cite[Section 4]{Tonita}):
\begin{equation}
J_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}:=(1-\tau)\sum_{d\geq 0}q^d\left\langle\frac{\phi_\alpha}{1-\tau L_1}\right\rangle^{\mathfrak{C}(E)}_{0,1,d} \, \phi^\alpha.
\end{equation}
The variable $\tau$ is typically denoted $q$ elsewhere; here we use $\tau$ to avoid confusion with Novikov variables. 


The quasimap counterpart of this function is the (twisted) small $I$-function, denoted $I_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}$ (defined originally in \cite{kquasimap}, and with twistings in \cite[Section 2]{wallcrossing}), which is defined as follows:
\begin{equation}\label{E:I-function-graph}
I_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}:=1-\tau + (1-\tau)(1-\tau^{-1})\sum_{d} \frac{q^d}{\mathfrak{C}(E)} ev_{0*} \left( \frac{\mathcal{O}^{vir}_{F_{0,d}}\otimes T_{(\mathfrak{C},E)}|_{F_{0,d}}}{Eu_\tau(N_{0,d})} \right).
\end{equation}
 Here $F_{0,d}, N_{0,d}$ were defined in section \ref{sec:qmaps}, and 
 $ev_0:F_{0,d}\to V//G$ is the evaluation map at the distinguished marked 
 point denoted $0$ earlier. 
 Note that the fixed locus $F_{0,d}$ inherits a perfect obstruction theory from the quasimap graph space, and thus has a well-defined virtual structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}^{vir}_{F_{0,d}}$. 

The definitions of these functions vary in the literature, with 
some omitting the factor of $(1-\tau)$. For the purposes of considering 
$\tau$-difference operators, we also add the following logarithmic prefactor. Let
$\{ P_i \}$ be the collection of line bundles determined by the fact that 
$-c_1(P_i)$ is dual to the Novikov variables $q_i$ for each $i$. Then we add the prefactor
$$P_i^{\log(q_i)/\log(\tau)} \/.$$ 
We will denote functions that have received this modification in boldface. In particular,
$$\mathbf{I}_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}:=\prod_i P_i^{\log(q_i)/\log(\tau)}I_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)},$$
$$\mathbf{J}_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}:=\prod_iP_i^{\log(q_i)/\log(\tau)}J_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}\/.$$
The advantage of adding the prefactor is that it transforms polynomials $f(P_i\tau^{q_i\partial_{q_i}})$ in products of factors $P_i \tau^{q_i\partial_{q_i}}$ into polynomials $f(\tau^{q_i\partial_{q_i}})$ involving only the difference operators
$\tau^{q_i\partial_{q_i}}$, which are easier to work with:
\begin{equation} \label{E:diff-prefactor}
f(P_i\tau^{q_i\partial_{q_i}})\prod_i P_i^{\log(q_i)/\log(\tau)}=\prod_i P_i^{\log(q_i)/\log(\tau)}f(\tau^{q_i\partial_{q_i}}).
\end{equation}




\begin{remark} The prefactor may also be interpreted as a formal Taylor expansion. More precisely,
write
\[ P_i^{\log(q_i)/\log(\tau)} = (1-(1-P_i))^{\log(q_i)/\log(\tau)} . \]
Using the formal Taylor expansion
\[ (1-x)^\alpha = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \binom{\alpha}{k}x^k \/, \quad \textrm{ where }\quad  \binom{\alpha}{k}:=\frac{\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(\alpha-i)}{k!} \/,\] 
we substitute $\alpha=\frac{\log(q_i)}{\log(\tau)}$, and $x=P_i-1$. 
Non-equiviariantly, the expansion is well-defined since $P_i-1$ is nilpotent. 
When working $T$-equivariantly, the expression only becomes well-defined after 
completing the ground algebra with respect to the $T$-equivariant parameters.
\end{remark}



The primary connection between the small $J$-function and the stable-map quantum $K$-theory rings is given by the following theorem due to Iritani, Milanov, and Tonita \cite{IMT} in the untwisted case, and generalized to the twisted case in \cite{HK1}:

\begin{thm}\label{twisted-imt}
    Let $D(\tau^{q_i\partial_{q_i}},\tau)$ be a polynomial $\tau-$difference operator annihilating $\mathbf{J}_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}$. Then
    $$D(\hat{P}_i,1)=0\in QK^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}_{T}(X)\/,$$
    where $\hat{P}_i$ are multiplication operators quantizing the multiplication by the line bundles $P_i$, and defined as solutions to a certain Lax equation.
\end{thm}

In other words, symbols of $\tau$-difference operators annihilating $\mathbf{J}$ become (after specializing $\tau\to 1$), yield relations in quantum $K$-theory. 


It was observed by Anderson, Chen, Tseng and Iritani in \cite[Lemma 6+]{act} that under certain conditions, the quantizations $\hat{P}_i$ are trivial, i.e., $\hat{P}_i=P_i$. A general statement valid for twisted invariants is available in \cite{HK1}, and reads as follows:


\begin{thm}\label{unhat} 
Write $J^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}=(1-\tau)\sum_{d} q^d J_d$. Fix some $i$. If for all nonzero effective curve classes $d=(d_1,\dots,d_k)$, 
$$\lim_{\tau\to \infty} \tau^{d_i} J_d=0\/,$$
then $\hat{P}_i=P_i$.
\end{thm}



\subsection{Notational conventions}
For further use, we establish some conventions regarding twistings.
Note that, in this work, we only consider two kinds of twistings, or compositions thereof: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item Ruan-Zhang level structures. The ones appearing in this paper are determined by a set of bundles $(E_1,\dots,E_n)$ and an integer vector $\ell=(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n)$. 

The choice of bundles will be clear from context, so we denote both the $I$ and $J$-functions, and the quantum $K$-ring of $X$ with this choice of level structure by  $I_X^\ell$, $J_X^\ell$, and $QK^\ell(X)$, respectively.


\item Twistings by the equivariant Euler class of the root bundle on the abelianization of a GIT quotient. We will denote quantum $K$-rings with this twisting by $QK^{tw}(X)$, and we denote the corresponding $I$-functions as $\widehat{I}_{Ab}$. 

\item In the presence of both twistings, we denote the corresponding rings as $QK^{tw,\ell}(X)$, and the $I$-functions as $\widehat{I}_{Ab}^\ell$.
\end{enumerate}



\subsection{Some technical results}
\label{sect:tech}

In this section we collect some technical results that will be used in the main text.
Proofs will appear in \cite{leoirittoappear}. 



The twisted small $I$ and $J$ functions $I^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}$, $J^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}$ are defined as follows:
\begin{equation}\label{E:IXCE}
I_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}:=1-\tau + (1-\tau)(1-\tau^{-1})\sum_{d} \frac{q^d}{\mathfrak{C}(E)} ev_{0*} \left( \frac{\mathcal{O}^{vir}_{F_{0,d}}\otimes T_{(\mathfrak{C},E)}|_{F_{0,d}}}{Eu_\tau(N_{0,d})} \right) \/;
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{E:JXCE}
J_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}:=1-\tau + (1-\tau)\sum_{d,\alpha} q^d \left\langle\frac{\phi_\alpha}{1-\tau L}\right\rangle^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}_{0,1,d}\phi^\alpha \/.
\end{equation}
Note that $I_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}$ is well defined, due to our hypothesis that $\mathfrak{C}(E)$ is invertible.


The following is the key fact needed in this paper. Variants of it are available in the literature (see, e.g., the proof of \cite[Theorem 2.6]{GY}), but it was not stated in the exact language  necessary for our purposes. 
We present only a brief outline of a proof, as a full description would take us too far afield. A full proof will appear in \cite{leoirittoappear}. 


\begin{thm}\label{thm:I=J}
Let $X=V//G$ a GIT quotient (possibly with a torus action), and recall the twisted small $I$ and $J$ functions {defined in
\eqref{E:IXCE} and \eqref{E:JXCE}, respectively. Write
$$I_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}=(1-\tau)\sum_d q^d I_d\/.$$
Then the equality of (torus-equivariant) twisted small $I$ and $J$ functions}: 
%statement
$$I_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}=J_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}$$
 is equivalent to the following conditions:
   \begin{enumerate}
    \item $I_d$ has no poles at $\tau=0$, and,
    \item For $d=0$, $I_d=1$, otherwise $deg_\tau(I_d)<-1$. 
    \end{enumerate}
\end{thm}


\begin{proof}[Sketch of proof]
This result follows from the wall-crossing formula of Zhang-Zhou \cite{wallcrossing}, which states that $I_X^{(\mathfrak{C},E)}$ is a point on the $S_n$-equivariant Lagrangian cone of $X$ twisted by $(\mathfrak{C},E)$. By the considerations in the proof of \cite[Theorem 2.6]{GY}, for this point to represent the twisted small $J$-function, it must satisfy the enumerated conditions. 
\end{proof}

Choose a Ruan-Zhang level structure on $V//G$ given by the bundles $E_i$, coming from $G$-representations $R_i$ on $V$, with levels $\ell_i$. Let $I^\ell_{V//G}$ denote the $I$-function of this theory. Let $\tilde{E}_i$ denote the bundle on $V//A$ induced by $R_i$. Let $L_\alpha$ denote the line bundles coming from the roots of $G$ relative to $A$.

\begin{defn}\label{ihat}
    The abelianized $I$-function $\widehat{I}_{Ab}^\ell$, is defined in the following way. Let $I_{V//A}^\ell$ be the $I$-function of $V//A$, with level structure determined by the bundles $\tilde{E}_i$ and levels $\ell_i$. 

    If $I_{V//A}^\ell=(1-\tau)\sum_{d} q^d I_d$, then:
    $$\widehat{I}_{Ab}:=(1-\tau)\sum_{d}q^d I_d \prod_\alpha \frac{\prod_{m=0}^{(c_1(L_\alpha),d)} (1-\lambda L_\alpha q^m)}{\prod_{m=-\infty}^{0} (1-\lambda L_\alpha q^m)} .$$
   
\end{defn}

\begin{thm}
$\widehat{I}_{Ab}^\ell$ is the $I$-function of $V//A$ with the following twistings:

 \begin{enumerate}

(A proof will be given in the upcoming paper \cite{leoirittoappear}.)

 \\
